source_text: Igitur si probos quosque seruos et bonae mentis pro ingenio dominico conuersari uidemus, - siquidem artificium promerendi obsequium est, obsequii uero disciplina morigera subiectio est — quanto magis nos secundum dominum moratos inueniri oportet, seruos scilicet dei uiui, cuius iudicium in suos non in compede aut pilleo uertitur, sed in aeternitate aut poenae aut salutis? cui seueritati declinandae uel liberalitati inuitandae tanta obsequii diligentia opus est, quanta sunt ipsa, quae aut seueritas comminatur aut liberalitas pollicetur. et tamen nos non de hominibus modo seruitute subnexis uel quolibet alio iure debitoribus obsequii, uerum etiam de pecudibus, etiam de bestiis oboedientiam exprimimus, intellegentes usibus nostris eas a domino prouisas traditasque. meliora ergo nobis erunt in obsequii disciplina quae nobis deus subdit? agnoscunt denique fl. quae oboediunt: nos cui soli subditi sumus, domino scilicet, auscultare dubitamus? at quam iniustum est, quam etiam ingratum, quod per alterius indulgentiam de aliis consequaris, idem illi, per quem consequeris, de temetipso non rependere! nec pluribus de obsequii exhibitione debiti a nobis domino deo. satis enim agnitio dei, quid sibi incumbat, intellegit. ne . tamen ut extraneum de obsequio uideamur interfecisse, ipsum quoque obsequium de patientia trahitur. numquis non\' patiens obsequitur aut patiens obluctatur? quam ergo dominus deus, omnium bonorum et demonstrator et acceptator, in semetipso circumtulit, quis de bono eius late retractet? cui item dubium sit omne bonum, quia ad deum pertineat, pertinentibus ad deum tota mente sectandum? per quae in expedito et quasi in praescriptionis compendio [et commendatio et exhortatio] de patientia constitutum est.
thought_title: Obedience owed to God is drawn from patience
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that if even slaves and animals obey their masters, how much more must Christians obey God, and that this obedience itself comes from patience.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if we see all good slaves and those of good mind conducting themselves according to the character of their master, since indeed the art of deserving is obedience, and the discipline of obedience is compliant subjection, how much more ought we to be found behaving according to the Lord, namely as slaves of the living God, whose judgment upon his own turns not on a shackle or a cap, but on eternity either of punishment or of salvation? For avoiding this severity or inviting this generosity, so great diligence of obedience is needed as are those very things which either the severity threatens or the generosity promises. And yet we exact obedience not only from men bound in slavery or debtors of obedience by any other law, but even from cattle, even from beasts, understanding that they have been provided and handed over by the Lord for our uses. Will those things which God subjects to us therefore be better than us in the discipline of obedience? Finally they recognize [their master] and obey: do we hesitate to listen to the one alone to whom we are subjected, namely the Lord? But how unjust it is, how ungrateful also, that what you obtain from others through another's indulgence, you should not repay from your very self to that same one through whom you obtain it! No more need be said about the rendering of obedience owed by us to the Lord God. For the knowledge of God understands what is incumbent upon itself. But lest we seem to have inserted something extraneous about obedience, obedience itself also is drawn from patience. Does anyone who is not patient obey, or does a patient person struggle against it? Therefore what the Lord God, the demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, carried around in himself, who would draw back from the good of it? To whom likewise would it be doubtful that every good, because it pertains to God, is to be pursued with the whole mind by those pertaining to God? Through these things it has been established about patience in a summary and as if in a compendium of prescription, both as commendation and exhortation.

choices.why: Keeps the two nouns distinct and renders morigerus as an adjective of compliance, matching the sense of dutiful submissiveness in the discipline of obedience.

choices.english: on a shackle or a cap
choices.why: Literal rendering preserves the concrete Roman markers of slave status (shackle) and freedman status (cap), which Tertullian contrasts with God's eternal judgment.
Renders the divine liberality that promises salvation, keeping the contrast with severity sharp and literal.
Preserves the objective genitive force: the knowledge that recognizes God and understands what is owed to him.

choices.term: in expedito et quasi in praescriptionis compendio
choices.english: in a summary and as if in a compendium of prescription
choices.why: Keeps the legal metaphor of praescriptio (a preliminary plea or rule) and the idea of brevity, matching Tertullian's rhetorical framing.
rejected: in brief and as a short rule

pass_b_english: So if we see every good and right-minded slave behaving according to his master's character—since the art of earning favor is obedience, and the discipline of obedience is compliant subjection—how much more should we be found conducting ourselves according to the Lord, as slaves of the living God, whose judgment on his own turns not on a shackle or a cap, but on an eternity either of punishment or of salvation? To avoid that severity or to be invited by that generosity requires as much diligence in obedience as the things themselves which the severity threatens or the generosity promises. And yet we exact obedience not only from human beings bound in slavery or indebted to obedience by any other right, but even from cattle, even from wild beasts, understanding that they have been provided and handed over to us by the Lord for our uses. Will the things God subjects to us, then, be better for us in the discipline of obedience? In short, the creatures that obey acknowledge their masters. Do we hesitate to listen to the one to whom alone we are subject, the Lord? How unjust it is, how ungrateful too, that what you obtain from others through another's kindness you should not repay to the very one through whom you obtain it, from your own self! No more need be said about rendering the obedience we owe to the Lord God. For the knowledge of God understands what is incumbent upon it. But so that we do not seem to have introduced obedience as something foreign, obedience itself is drawn from patience. Does anyone who is impatient obey, or anyone who is patient resist? What the Lord God, the demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, has surrounded himself with—who would draw back from its good? Who likewise could doubt that every good, because it belongs to God, is to be pursued with the whole mind by those who belong to God? Through these things, in a summary and as if in a compendium of prescription, both the commendation and the exhortation concerning patience have been established.
notes: The source text contains 'agnoscunt denique fl.' with 'fl.' apparently an abbreviation or damage; the gloss renders it as 'they recognize [their master]' based on context, but the exact word is uncertain.
The phrase 'ne . tamen ut extraneum' contains a gap or punctuation anomaly; the gloss renders the sense as 'but lest we seem to have inserted something extraneous'.

problems.quote: or struggle against it with patience
problems.why: Source means 'or does a patient person struggle (against obedience)?' The English makes patience the thing struggled against.
problems.fix: or does a patient person struggle against it?
problems.ruling: Latin: ‘aut patiens obluctatur’ = ‘or (does one) wrestle patiently’; English adds ‘against it’, altering meaning.

problems.quote: Will those whom God has subjected to us, then, be better than we are in the discipline of obedience?
problems.source_quote: meliora ergo nobis erunt in obsequii disciplina quae nobis deus subdit?
problems.why: Latin asks whether *better things* will be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us, not whether the subjects themselves will be better than us.
problems.fix: Will better things be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us?
problems.ruling: meliora nobis erunt = 'will things be better for us'; neuter plural subject, not 'will those...be better than we are'.

edits.old: or struggle against it with patience
edits.new: or does a patient person struggle against it?

edits.old: Will those whom God has subjected to us, then, be better than we are in the discipline of obedience?
edits.new: Will better things be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us?

fixed: Corrected 'or struggle against it with patience' to 'or does a patient person struggle against it?' because the source 'aut patiens obluctatur' asks whether a patient person struggles against obedience, not whether patience is struggled against.

Corrected 'Will those whom God has subjected to us, then, be better than we are in the discipline of obedience?' to 'Will better things be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us?' because the source 'meliora ergo nobis erunt in obsequii disciplina quae nobis deus subdit?' asks whether better things will be for us, not whether the subjects themselves will be better than us.

problems.quote: Will better things be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us?
problems.source_quote: meliora ergo nobis erunt in obsequii disciplina quae nobis deus subdit?
problems.why: Source asks: will the things God subjects to us be better for us in the discipline of obedience? English misreads 'quae' as 'discipline' rather than 'things God subjects'.
problems.fix: Will the things God subjects to us, then, be better for us in the discipline of obedience?
problems.ruling: Latin 'quae nobis deus subdit' modifies 'meliora', not 'obsequii disciplina'; English attaches clause to 'discipline', misreading object.

problems.why: Source means 'even the animals that obey acknowledge [their masters]'; English drops the object and makes 'they' the animals themselves.
problems.fix: Even the animals that obey acknowledge their masters.
problems.ruling: 'agnoscunt denique fl. quae oboediunt' has object 'fl.' (animals) obeying; English makes subject obey, dropping object.

problems.quote: Who, then, would question at length the good of that which the Lord God, the demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, carried about in himself?
problems.source_quote: quam ergo dominus deus, omnium bonorum et demonstrator et acceptator, in semetipso circumtulit, quis de bono eius late retractet?
problems.why: 'late retractet' means 'would treat at length/withdraw'; 'de bono eius' = 'concerning his good'. English garbles the clause structure.
problems.fix: What good the Lord God, demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, carried about in himself—who would treat at length concerning his good?
problems.ruling: 'qui de bono eius late retractet' = who would withdraw about his good; English renders as 'question at length' and mis‑parses 'circumtulit'.

edits.old: Will better things be for us in the discipline of obedience that God has subjected to us?
edits.new: Will the things God subjects to us, then, be better for us in the discipline of obedience?

edits.old: In short, they acknowledge that they obey.
edits.new: In short, even the animals that obey acknowledge their masters.

fixed: Corrected 'Will better things be for us...' to 'Will the things God subjects to us, then, be better for us...' because the source 'quae nobis deus subdit' refers to the things God subjects, not to the discipline.

Corrected 'they acknowledge that they obey' to 'even the animals that obey acknowledge their masters' because the source 'agnoscunt denique fl. quae oboediunt' means the animals that obey acknowledge their masters.

Corrected 'Who, then, would question at length the good of that which...' to 'What good the Lord God... carried about in himself—who would treat at length concerning his good?' because the source 'quam... circumtulit, quis de bono eius late retractet?' has 'quam' as the object of 'circumtulit' and 'de bono eius' as the object of 'retractet'.

problems.quote: What good the Lord God, the demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, carried about in himself—who would treat at length concerning his good?
problems.source_quote: quam ergo dominus deus, omnium bonorum et demonstrator et acceptator, in semetipso circumtulit, quis de bono eius late retractet?
problems.why: Latin says God has “circumtulit” (surrounded) himself with all good; the English renders it as “carried about in himself,” which misstates the image and adds unrelated phrasing.
problems.fix: What then the Lord God, demonstrator and acceptor of all good things, has surrounded himself with—who could retract anything concerning his good?

problems.quote: the animals that obey acknowledge their masters
problems.why: 'fl.' is an abbreviation for 'filii' (sons), not animals. The clause means 'sons acknowledge what they obey.'
problems.fix: In short, sons acknowledge what they obey
problems.ruling: 'fl.' abbreviates filios (sons), not animals; translation says 'animals', changing the meaning.

problems.quote: Does anyone obey without patience, or does a patient person struggle against it??
problems.source_quote: numquis non' patiens obsequitur aut patiens obliter?
problems.why: The Latin contrasts obeying patiently with obeying without patience; "obliter" (to destroy) is not “struggle against it.” The English changes the meaning.
problems.fix: Does anyone not obey patiently, or does a patient person obey without patience?
problems.ruling: Source says 'patiens obluctatur' (patient person struggles/resists), but English 'obliter' misread changes meaning.

fixed: Corrected 'carried about in himself' to 'has surrounded himself with' to match 'circumtulit' and removed the unrelated 'treat at length' phrasing.
Corrected 'the animals that obey acknowledge their masters' to 'sons acknowledge what they obey' to match 'fl. quae oboediunt' (filii).
Corrected the patience/obedience contrast to match 'numquis non patiens obsequitur aut patiens obluctatur'.

fixed.quote: In short, sons acknowledge what they obey.
fixed.fix: In short, the creatures that obey acknowledge their masters.
fixed.note: The abbreviation 'fl.' is corrupt (editions read 'illa'), and the context is animals that obey. 'Sons' has no support in the text.

fixed.quote: Does anyone not obey patiently, or does a patient person obey without patience?
fixed.fix: Does anyone who is impatient obey, or anyone who is patient resist?
fixed.note: 'Non patiens' means 'impatient' and 'obluctatur' means 'resists'. The English garbles both, and the proposed fix is also wrong.

dismissed.quote: we exact obedience not only from human beings bound in slavery or indebted to obedience by any other right, but even from cattle, even from wild beasts, understanding that they have been provided and handed over to us by the Lord for our uses.
dismissed.why: Latin says we express obedience toward animals; English says we demand/exact obedience from them, reversing agency.
dismissed.note: 'Oboedientiam exprimimus' means 'we squeeze out' or exact obedience from them, so the English agency is correct.
